Lesson 1 · C1.1.1 – C1.1.4 · SL & HL

Enzymes as Catalysts & Metabolism

Why can't life happen without enzymes – and how do they control what a cell does?

By the end you can

  • Explain the benefit to cells of enzymes increasing reaction rates.
  • Describe metabolism as a network of enzyme-controlled reactions and explain why many enzymes are needed.
  • Distinguish anabolic and catabolic reactions using IB examples.
  • Describe enzymes as globular proteins with an active site held in shape by the whole 3D structure.

Key terms

catalystenzymemetabolismmetabolitemetabolic pathwayanabolismcatabolismcondensationhydrolysisglobular proteinactive site

C1.1.1

Enzymes as catalysts

  • A catalyst speeds up a chemical reaction without being used up or permanently changed.
  • Enzymes are biological catalysts – almost all are globular proteins (a few are RNA, called ribozymes).
  • Most reactions in cells would happen far too slowly at body temperature (≈37 °C) and near-neutral pH to keep an organism alive.
  • Cells cannot speed reactions up by heating, raising pressure or using extreme pH – these would denature proteins and damage the cell.
  • Enzymes increase reaction rates by thousands to millions of times at normal body conditions (one catalase molecule can break down millions of H₂O₂ molecules per second).
  • Enzymes are reusable, so only small amounts are needed.
  • Benefit to the cell: vital reactions (e.g. respiration, DNA replication, removing toxic H₂O₂) happen fast enough to sustain life.

Memory hookCAT-alyst → Changes the rate · Always reused · Tiny amounts needed

Worked example

Hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂) is a toxic by-product of metabolism. A bottle of H₂O₂ decomposes slowly over months, but in liver cells it is destroyed in a fraction of a second. Explain the benefit of catalase to the cell. [2]

Show answer
  • Catalase is a catalyst that greatly increases the rate of H₂O₂ breakdown (into water and oxygen) ✓
  • so toxic H₂O₂ is removed before it can damage cell components / at body temperature without denaturing cell proteins ✓

C1.1.2

Role of enzymes in metabolism

  • Metabolism = the complex network of interdependent and interacting chemical reactions that occur in a living organism.
  • Molecules taking part in these reactions are called metabolites.
  • Many reactions occur as metabolic pathways – a series of small steps, each catalysed by a different, specific enzyme.
  • Pathways are interlinked: the product of one pathway may be the substrate of another, so a change in one affects others.
  • Enzymes are specific (usually one enzyme catalyses one reaction), so organisms need thousands of different enzymes.
  • Control of metabolism is exerted through enzymes: the cell can (1) choose which enzymes to make (gene expression) and (2) change their activity (e.g. inhibitors, activators).
  • No enzyme → no (significant) reaction. So enzymes act like switches that decide which reactions happen in which cell.

Memory hookMAC: Metabolism = Anabolism + Catabolism

Worked example

Explain why living organisms need many different enzymes. [2]

Show answer
  • Enzymes are specific: each active site is complementary to (fits) only one / a few substrates ✓
  • metabolism involves thousands of different reactions, so a different enzyme is needed for each reaction ✓

C1.1.3

Anabolic and catabolic reactions

  • ANABOLISM – building larger molecules (macromolecules) from smaller ones (monomers).
  • Anabolic reactions are usually condensation reactions (water is released) and require energy (often from ATP).
  • Examples: protein synthesis (amino acids → polypeptide, peptide bonds); glycogen formation (α-glucose → glycogen, glycosidic bonds); photosynthesis (CO₂ + H₂O → glucose).
  • CATABOLISM – breaking larger molecules down into smaller ones.
  • Catabolic reactions include hydrolysis (water is used) and oxidation; they release energy.
  • Examples: hydrolysis of macromolecules into monomers in digestion (starch → maltose/glucose; protein → amino acids; triglycerides → fatty acids + glycerol); oxidation of substrates in respiration (glucose → CO₂ + H₂O).
  • Both anabolism and catabolism are catalysed by enzymes, and they are linked by ATP: catabolism releases energy that is used to make ATP; anabolism uses ATP.
AnabolismCatabolism
What happensBuilds macromolecules from monomersBreaks large molecules into smaller ones
Typical reactionCondensation (water released)Hydrolysis (water used) / oxidation
EnergyRequired (endergonic)Released (exergonic)
IB examplesProtein synthesis, glycogen formation, photosynthesisDigestion of macromolecules, respiration

Memory hookAnabolic = Assemble (Add) · Catabolic = Cut (Crumble)

Worked example

Classify the formation of glycogen in the liver and the digestion of starch in the small intestine as anabolic or catabolic, and name the type of reaction involved in each. [2]

Show answer
  • Glycogen formation is anabolic – condensation reactions link α-glucose monomers ✓
  • Starch digestion is catabolic – hydrolysis reactions split starch into maltose/glucose ✓

C1.1.4

Enzymes as globular proteins with an active site

  • Enzymes are globular proteins: polypeptide chains folded into a compact, roughly spherical tertiary (sometimes quaternary) structure; usually soluble in water.
  • The active site is the region where the substrate binds and catalysis happens.
  • The active site is made of only a few amino acids (their R-groups line the site).
  • BUT the whole 3D structure matters: interactions between amino acids throughout the enzyme (hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds, disulfide bridges, hydrophobic interactions) hold the active site in its exact shape.
  • These interactions also give the active site the right chemical properties (charge, polarity) to bind the substrate and catalyse the reaction.
  • Consequence: a change to an amino acid far from the active site (e.g. after a mutation) can still change the shape of the active site and stop the enzyme working.

Memory hookFew to bind, all to hold: a FEW amino acids form the site, ALL the others hold it in shape.

Worked example

A mutation replaces one amino acid located far from the active site of an enzyme. The enzyme no longer catalyses its reaction. Suggest why. [3]

Show answer
  • The R-group of the new amino acid forms different bonds / interactions ✓
  • so the tertiary (3D) structure of the enzyme changes ✓
  • which alters the shape/chemical properties of the active site so the substrate no longer binds ✓

Lesson 2 · C1.1.5 – C1.1.7, C1.1.10 · SL & HL

How Enzymes Work: Induced Fit, Collisions, Specificity & Activation Energy

How does an enzyme actually make a reaction go faster – and why does it stop working when heated?

By the end you can

  • Describe induced-fit binding, recognising that both substrate and enzyme change shape.
  • Explain the role of molecular motion and collisions, including immobilised substrates and enzymes.
  • Explain the links between active-site structure, specificity and denaturation.
  • Interpret energy graphs showing how enzymes lower activation energy.

Key terms

induced fitlock-and-keyconformational changeenzyme–substrate complexcollisionorientationimmobilised enzymespecificitydenaturationactivation energytransition state

C1.1.5

Induced-fit binding

  • Lock-and-key model (Fischer, 1894): active site is rigid and exactly complementary to the substrate.
  • Induced-fit model (Koshland, 1958) – the current model: both the substrate AND the enzyme change shape when binding occurs.
  • As the substrate enters, the active site moulds around it (a conformational change), forming a tight enzyme–substrate complex.
  • This change puts strain on bonds in the substrate, helping it reach the transition state – this is how catalysis happens.
  • When products leave, the enzyme returns to its original shape and can be reused.
  • NOS: models are replaced or refined when new evidence appears (X-ray crystallography shows enzymes such as hexokinase closing around their substrate).

Memory hookLock-and-key = key in lock (rigid) · Induced fit = hand in a glove (both adjust)

Worked example

Distinguish between the lock-and-key and induced-fit models of enzyme action. [2]

Show answer
  • Lock-and-key: active site has a fixed/rigid shape exactly complementary to the substrate ✓
  • Induced fit: enzyme and substrate both change shape on binding / active site moulds around the substrate, stressing its bonds ✓

C1.1.6

Molecular motion and substrate–active site collisions

  • Molecules in solution have kinetic energy and move randomly.
  • For a reaction, the substrate must collide with the active site in the correct orientation (and with enough energy) – a successful collision.
  • A successful collision forms an enzyme–substrate complex; unsuccessful collisions just bounce off.
  • Usually substrate molecules move more than enzymes because they are smaller.
  • Sometimes a large substrate is immobilised (e.g. a starch grain or a cellulose fibre) and the enzymes move to it.
  • Sometimes enzymes are immobilised by being embedded in membranes (e.g. ATP synthase in the inner mitochondrial membrane; maltase and other enzymes in the membranes of intestinal microvilli) – the substrate moves to them.
  • Industry also immobilises enzymes (e.g. lactase in alginate beads for lactose-free milk): enzymes are reused and do not contaminate the product.

Memory hookCollide · Correct orientation · Complex forms

Worked example

Explain why an increase in temperature from 20 °C to 30 °C increases the rate of an enzyme-catalysed reaction. [3]

Show answer
  • Molecules gain kinetic energy / move faster ✓
  • so substrate collides with the active site more frequently ✓
  • more enzyme–substrate complexes form per unit time / more collisions have enough energy ✓

C1.1.7

Active site structure, specificity and denaturation

  • Specificity: the shape and chemical properties of the active site are complementary to one substrate (or a small group of similar substrates).
  • So the structure of the enzyme → shape/chemistry of the active site → which substrate it binds (specificity).
  • Denaturation: a permanent change in the 3D (tertiary) structure of a protein caused by high temperature or extreme pH.
  • Heat makes the molecule vibrate so much that hydrogen bonds and ionic bonds between R-groups break; extreme pH changes the charges on R-groups, breaking ionic and hydrogen bonds.
  • Peptide bonds are NOT broken – the primary structure stays the same.
  • The active site changes shape → substrate no longer fits/binds → no catalysis. Denatured enzymes often become insoluble.
  • Denaturation is usually irreversible. Low temperature does NOT denature – it only slows the enzyme down.

Memory hookShape → Site → Specificity. Break the shape, lose the site.

Worked example

Explain how a high temperature affects enzyme activity. [3]

Show answer
  • Bonds holding the tertiary structure (hydrogen/ionic bonds) break due to increased vibration ✓
  • the active site changes shape / enzyme is denatured ✓
  • substrate can no longer bind / fewer enzyme–substrate complexes so rate falls ✓

C1.1.10

Effect of enzymes on activation energy

  • Activation energy = the energy needed to break bonds in the substrate so that the reaction can start (to reach the transition state).
  • Energy is required to break bonds within the substrate; energy is released (an energy yield) when new bonds form to make the products.
  • In an exergonic reaction the products have less energy than the substrates – overall energy is released.
  • Enzymes LOWER the activation energy: binding (induced fit) strains/weakens bonds in the substrate and holds reacting groups in the correct position.
  • So more molecules have enough energy to react at body temperature → faster reaction.
  • Enzymes do NOT change the overall energy change (ΔG) of the reaction or the energy of the substrates and products.
  • Reading graphs: height from substrate level to peak = activation energy; difference between substrate and product levels = net energy released.

Memory hookEnzymes lower the hill, not the drop.

Worked example

On an energy diagram, the substrate is at 60 kJ, the peak without enzyme is at 140 kJ, the peak with enzyme is at 90 kJ and the products are at 20 kJ. Calculate (a) activation energy with enzyme, (b) net energy released. [2]

Show answer
  • (a) 90 − 60 = 30 kJ ✓
  • (b) 60 − 20 = 40 kJ released (same with or without enzyme) ✓

Lesson 3 · C1.1.8 – C1.1.9 · SL & HL

Factors Affecting Enzyme Activity & Measuring Reaction Rates

How do temperature, pH and substrate concentration change the rate of an enzyme-catalysed reaction – and how do we measure it?

By the end you can

  • Explain the effects of temperature, pH and substrate concentration using collision theory and denaturation.
  • Interpret and sketch graphs of enzyme activity; recognise sketch graphs as models (NOS).
  • Determine reaction rates from experiments and secondary data, including initial rate from a tangent.

Key terms

optimum temperatureoptimum pHkinetic energycollision theorydenaturationsaturationlimiting factorrate of reactiontangentinitial rate

C1.1.8

Effect of temperature

  • Below the optimum: as temperature rises, molecules gain kinetic energy → more frequent successful collisions between substrate and active site → more enzyme–substrate complexes → rate increases (roughly doubles for every 10 °C rise).
  • Optimum temperature: the temperature at which the rate is highest (≈37–40 °C for most human enzymes).
  • Above the optimum: vibrations break hydrogen and ionic bonds in the tertiary structure → active site changes shape → denaturation → rate falls steeply.
  • The curve is not symmetrical: the fall after the optimum is much steeper than the rise.
  • At low temperatures the enzyme is inactive but not denatured – activity returns on warming.
  • Enzymes from thermophiles have high optimums (e.g. Taq polymerase from hot-spring bacteria works at ≈72 °C).

Memory hookRise = collisions · Fall = denaturation

C1.1.8

Effect of pH

  • pH measures hydrogen ion (H⁺) concentration; it is a logarithmic scale – each 1 unit change = 10× change in [H⁺].
  • Each enzyme has an optimum pH where the active site has the ideal shape and charge.
  • Either side of the optimum, changes in [H⁺] alter the charges on R-groups in the active site → substrate binds less well → rate falls.
  • At extreme pH, ionic and hydrogen bonds in the tertiary structure break → denaturation.
  • Optimum depends on where the enzyme works: pepsin (stomach) ≈ pH 2; salivary amylase ≈ pH 7; trypsin (small intestine) ≈ pH 8.
  • pH curves are usually roughly bell-shaped (symmetrical) around the optimum.

Memory hookpH changes Charges → Changes binding

C1.1.8

Effect of substrate concentration

  • With a fixed amount of enzyme, increasing substrate concentration increases the frequency of collisions with active sites → rate increases.
  • At low concentrations rate rises steeply (nearly proportional) – substrate is the limiting factor.
  • As concentration rises further, more active sites are occupied at any moment, so the rate rises more slowly.
  • Eventually all active sites are occupied (saturated) → the curve plateaus at the maximum rate.
  • On the plateau, adding substrate has no effect – enzyme concentration is now the limiting factor; adding more enzyme would raise the rate.
  • NOS: these generalised sketch graphs are models; they can be tested and evaluated against real experimental results.

Memory hookMore substrate → more collisions … until every seat (active site) is taken.

Worked example

Describe and explain the effect of substrate concentration on the rate of an enzyme-catalysed reaction. [4]

Show answer
  • As substrate concentration increases, rate increases (steeply at first) ✓
  • because more frequent collisions with active sites / more ES complexes ✓
  • rate levels off / plateaus at high substrate concentration ✓
  • because all active sites are occupied/saturated – enzyme concentration becomes limiting ✓

C1.1.9

Measuring rates of enzyme-catalysed reactions

  • Rate = amount of product formed (or substrate used) ÷ time. Units, e.g. cm³ s⁻¹ or mg min⁻¹.
  • If you only measure the time taken to reach an end-point, rate = 1 ÷ time (units s⁻¹).
  • Catalase: 2H₂O₂ → 2H₂O + O₂. Measure the volume of oxygen (gas syringe or upturned measuring cylinder) or count bubbles / time disc flotation.
  • Amylase: starch → maltose. Test samples with iodine solution at intervals; record the time for blue-black to stop appearing (or use a colorimeter).
  • Initial rate: draw a tangent to the curve at t = 0 and find its gradient (Δy ÷ Δx) – this is the fastest rate, before substrate is used up.
  • The curve flattens because substrate is used up (not because the enzyme is used up).
  • Control variables: temperature (water bath), pH (buffer), volumes and concentrations of enzyme and substrate; repeat trials and calculate means.

Memory hookRate = change ÷ time · Initial rate = tangent at zero

Worked example

Using the catalase graph, the tangent at t = 0 passes through 71 cm³ at 20 s. Calculate the initial rate. [1] A second student timed the reaction to an end-point of 25 s. Calculate the rate as 1/t. [1]

Show answer
  • Initial rate = 71 ÷ 20 = 3.6 cm³ s⁻¹ (accept 3.5–3.6) ✓
  • Rate = 1 ÷ 25 = 0.04 s⁻¹ ✓

Lesson 4 · C1.1.11 – C1.1.13 · HL only (AHL)

Metabolism in Action: Where Enzymes Work, Heat & Pathways

Where do enzymes work, why does metabolism make us warm, and how are pathways organised?

By the end you can

  • Distinguish intracellular and extracellular enzymes, using glycolysis, the Krebs cycle and digestion as examples.
  • Explain why metabolism generates heat and how endotherms use it.
  • Compare linear and cyclical pathways using glycolysis, the Krebs cycle and the Calvin cycle.

Key terms

intracellularextracellularexocytosissecretory vesicleefficiencyendothermectothermlinear pathwaycyclical pathwayglycolysisKrebs cycleCalvin cycle

C1.1.11

Intracellular and extracellular enzymes

  • Intracellular enzymes are made and work inside the cell (cytoplasm or organelles).
  • Examples: enzymes of glycolysis (cytoplasm) and of the Krebs cycle (mitochondrial matrix).
  • Extracellular enzymes are made inside the cell but work outside it.
  • They are made on ribosomes of the rough ER, processed in the Golgi apparatus, packaged into vesicles and secreted by exocytosis.
  • Example: chemical digestion in the gut – amylase, pepsin, trypsin and lipase hydrolyse macromolecules in the lumen of the gut.
  • Fungi and many bacteria also secrete extracellular enzymes to digest food outside their cells (saprotrophic nutrition).

Memory hookINtra = INside · EXtra = EXported

Worked example

Outline the difference between intracellular and extracellular enzymes, with one example of each. [2]

Show answer
  • Intracellular enzymes catalyse reactions inside the cell, e.g. glycolysis/Krebs cycle enzymes ✓
  • extracellular enzymes are secreted and catalyse reactions outside the cell, e.g. digestive enzymes such as pepsin/amylase in the gut ✓

C1.1.12

Generation of heat by metabolism

  • Energy transfers in metabolic reactions are never 100% efficient – some energy is always converted to heat.
  • Example: in aerobic respiration only about a third of the energy in glucose ends up in ATP; the rest is released as heat.
  • So heat generation is inevitable in every living cell.
  • Mammals and birds (endotherms) depend on this metabolic heat to keep a constant, high body temperature.
  • When cold, endotherms raise their metabolic rate to generate more heat (e.g. shivering; brown adipose tissue).
  • Some other animals also use metabolic heat (e.g. bees warming flight muscles, tuna keeping swimming muscles warm).
  • Ectotherms (e.g. most reptiles, amphibians, fish) gain heat mainly from the environment; their metabolic rate rises and falls with environmental temperature.

Memory hookNo transfer is perfect → the lost energy keeps us warm.

Worked example

Explain why all metabolising cells release heat, and why this is important for mammals. [3]

Show answer
  • Energy transfers in metabolic reactions (e.g. respiration) are not 100% efficient ✓
  • the energy not transferred to useful products (e.g. ATP) is lost as heat ✓
  • mammals use this heat to maintain a constant body temperature (endothermy) ✓

C1.1.13

Cyclical and linear pathways

  • Linear pathway: a chain of reactions with a clear start (initial substrate) and end (final product); each step is catalysed by a specific enzyme.
  • Example: glycolysis (cytoplasm) – glucose → → → 2 pyruvate in ten enzyme-catalysed steps.
  • Cyclical pathway: the last step regenerates the starting compound, so the cycle can turn again and again.
  • Example 1: Krebs cycle (mitochondrial matrix) – an acetyl group (2C) joins oxaloacetate (4C) to make citrate (6C); CO₂ is released and oxaloacetate is regenerated.
  • Example 2: Calvin cycle (chloroplast stroma) – RuBP (5C) fixes CO₂ (catalysed by RuBisCO); triose phosphate is produced and RuBP is regenerated.
  • Advantage of cycles: a small amount of each intermediate is reused continuously, so the pathway keeps running as long as inputs are supplied.

Memory hookLinear = Line (start → finish) · Cycle = Circle (start comes back)

Worked example

Compare and contrast glycolysis and the Krebs cycle as metabolic pathways. [3]

Show answer
  • Both are series of enzyme-catalysed steps / both are part of cell respiration / both oxidise substrates ✓
  • glycolysis is linear (glucose → pyruvate) whereas the Krebs cycle is cyclical (oxaloacetate regenerated) ✓
  • glycolysis occurs in the cytoplasm, the Krebs cycle in the mitochondrial matrix ✓

Lesson 5 · C1.1.14 – C1.1.17 · HL only (AHL)

Controlling Enzymes: Inhibition & Feedback

How can cells and medicines switch enzymes off – temporarily or permanently?

By the end you can

  • Explain non-competitive inhibition via allosteric sites.
  • Explain competitive inhibition using statins and distinguish the two types by the effect of substrate concentration.
  • Explain feedback inhibition using the isoleucine pathway.
  • Explain mechanism-based inhibition using penicillin, including resistance.

Key terms

inhibitorallosteric sitenon-competitivecompetitivestatinHMG-CoA reductasefeedback inhibitionend productthreonine deaminaseisoleucinemechanism-based inhibitiontranspeptidasepenicillinresistance

C1.1.14

Allosteric sites and non-competitive inhibition

  • An allosteric site is a binding site on an enzyme away from the active site.
  • Only specific substances can bind to an allosteric site (complementary shape and chemistry).
  • Binding causes interactions within the enzyme that lead to a conformational change; this alters the active site enough to prevent catalysis.
  • Binding is reversible (weak bonds) – when the inhibitor leaves, the enzyme works again.
  • This is non-competitive inhibition: the inhibitor does not compete with the substrate for the active site.
  • So increasing substrate concentration does NOT overcome it – the maximum rate is lowered.
  • Example: ATP binds to an allosteric site of phosphofructokinase, an enzyme of glycolysis, slowing respiration when ATP is plentiful.

Memory hookALLO-steric = 'other' site → changes the shape elsewhere

C1.1.15

Competitive inhibition (statins)

  • A competitive inhibitor has a similar shape and chemistry to the substrate.
  • It binds reversibly to the active site, blocking the substrate from binding.
  • Substrate and inhibitor compete: the effect depends on their relative concentrations.
  • Increasing substrate concentration reduces the effect – at high substrate concentration the maximum rate is still reached.
  • Example – statins: competitive inhibitors of HMG-CoA reductase, a liver enzyme in the pathway that makes cholesterol.
  • Less cholesterol is synthesised → lower blood LDL cholesterol → reduced risk of atherosclerosis and coronary heart disease.
CompetitiveNon-competitive
Binds toActive siteAllosteric site
ShapeSimilar to substrateNot similar to substrate
How it inhibitsBlocks substrate from active siteChanges shape of active site
Effect of more substrateOvercomes inhibition – max rate reachedCannot overcome – max rate lowered
ExampleStatins (HMG-CoA reductase)Isoleucine on threonine deaminase; ATP on PFK

Memory hookCompetitive = Copycat in the Centre · Non-competitive = Not there, Nudges shape

Worked example

Explain why the effect of a competitive inhibitor, but not a non-competitive inhibitor, can be reduced by increasing substrate concentration. [3]

Show answer
  • Competitive inhibitor binds to the active site/competes with substrate ✓
  • more substrate molecules → substrate more likely to collide with/occupy active sites than inhibitor ✓
  • non-competitive inhibitor binds to an allosteric site changing the active site, so substrate cannot bind however much is added ✓

C1.1.16

Feedback (end-product) inhibition

  • In feedback inhibition the end product of a metabolic pathway inhibits an enzyme near the start (usually the first enzyme).
  • The end product usually acts as a non-competitive (allosteric) inhibitor.
  • When the end product is plentiful, the pathway slows → no wasted energy or raw materials; intermediates do not build up.
  • When the end product is used up, it detaches from the allosteric site → the enzyme works again → production restarts.
  • This is a negative feedback loop that keeps the end product at a steady level.
  • IB example: threonine → isoleucine in bacteria (5 enzyme-catalysed steps). Isoleucine binds to the allosteric site of threonine deaminase, the first enzyme.

Memory hookThe end product puts the brakes on the first enzyme.

Worked example

Explain how isoleucine regulates its own synthesis. [3]

Show answer
  • Isoleucine (end product) binds to the allosteric site of threonine deaminase, the first enzyme of the pathway ✓
  • this changes the shape of the active site so threonine cannot bind / pathway stops ✓
  • when isoleucine levels fall it detaches (reversible) and the pathway resumes – negative feedback ✓

C1.1.17

Mechanism-based inhibition (penicillin)

  • A mechanism-based inhibitor binds irreversibly (by a covalent bond) to the active site and chemically changes it → enzyme permanently inactivated.
  • Bacterial cell walls contain peptidoglycan: sugar chains joined by peptide cross-links, made by enzymes called transpeptidases.
  • Penicillin's shape resembles the end of the peptide that transpeptidase normally binds.
  • In the active site the β-lactam ring of penicillin opens and bonds covalently to the enzyme – the transpeptidase is permanently blocked.
  • Growing bacteria cannot form cross-links, so new cell wall is weak → water enters by osmosis → the cell bursts (lysis). Penicillin works only on bacteria that are growing.
  • Resistance: mutations change the active site of transpeptidase so penicillin no longer binds, while the enzyme can still make cross-links (e.g. MRSA).
  • Resistance genes can spread between bacteria on plasmids (conjugation). Human cells have no cell walls/transpeptidases, so penicillin does not harm them.

Memory hookPenicillin = Permanent: it Plugs the transPeptidase for good.

Worked example

Explain how a mutation in a bacterium can make it resistant to penicillin. [2]

Show answer
  • Mutation changes the amino acid sequence/shape of the transpeptidase active site ✓
  • penicillin can no longer bind, but the enzyme can still form cross-links, so the cell wall is still made ✓
